replacements.literal: Bin had ordering-the-realm great capacity, yet was not constrained by conduct and self-restraint.
replacements.idiomatic: Tang Bin had the breadth of mind to govern the realm but cared little for conventional propriety.

replacements.literal: In youth he was skilled at bow and horse, loved roaming and hunting; his body was eight *chi* tall, in running he caught up with fleeing deer; his strength doubled other men.
replacements.idiomatic: As a youth he excelled at riding and archery and loved the chase; he stood eight feet tall, could outrun a bolting stag, and possessed strength beyond ordinary men.

replacements.literal: Only in later years did he earnestly delight in the classics and histories; he was especially clear on the *Book of Changes*; he followed a teacher to receive instruction, returned home and taught; constantly there were several hundred persons.
replacements.idiomatic: Later he turned seriously to the classics and histories, with particular mastery of the *Zhou yi*; he studied under a tutor, then taught at home to an audience routinely numbering in the hundreds.

replacements.literal: At first he served as a clerk under the commandery’s gate, then was transferred to registrar.
replacements.idiomatic: He began as a junior clerk in the commandery administration and was promoted to chief registrar.

replacements.literal: The inspector Wang Shen assembled the various aides and staff, grandly discoursing on strategies to resist Wu, and put the question to the clerks of the nine commanderies.
replacements.idiomatic: Inspector Wang Shen convened his staff for a wide-ranging discussion of how to oppose Wu and polled the recorders of the nine commanderies.

replacements.literal: Bin together with Qiao commandery’s registrar Zhang Yun both set forth that Wu had a situation that could be annexed; Shen approved their replies.
replacements.idiomatic: Tang Bin and Zhang Yun, registrar of Qiao, both argued that Wu could be overrun; Wang Shen commended their answers.

replacements.literal: Again he had Bin challenge the words of those who said Wu could not yet be attacked, and in every case their wording and reasoning were bent [defeated].
replacements.idiomatic: He then had Tang Bin refute those who claimed Wu was not ripe for attack, and each opponent’s argument collapsed.

replacements.literal: He was returned [to office] and promoted merit evaluator; he was recommended filial and incorrupt; the province summoned him as registrar; by stages he rose to aide-de-camp.
replacements.idiomatic: He was moved up to merit evaluator, nominated filial and incorrupt, appointed provincial registrar, and eventually promoted to governor’s chief of staff.

replacements.literal: Bin was loyal, solemn, fair, and bright; he exhausted remonstrance and rescue; he did not display remonstrance to make himself conspicuous; moreover he was sent on mission to the minister’s office to plan affairs—at that time the aides and staff were all the age’s outstanding talents; seeing Bin, none failed to admire and delight, and they praised him to Emperor Wen and recommended him as a bureau subordinate.
replacements.idiomatic: Tang Bin was loyal, grave, and upright; he remonstrated tirelessly to set things right without parading his counsel for fame. Sent to the chancellor’s headquarters on business, he impressed every eminent man on staff, who spoke of him to Emperor Wen and secured him a post among the clerks.

replacements.literal: The emperor thereupon asked his army adviser Kong Hao; Hao envied his ability and for a long time did not answer.
replacements.idiomatic: The emperor turned to his adviser Kong Hao, who resented Tang Bin’s talent and remained silent.

replacements.literal: Chen Qian was seated; he gathered his tablet and declared, saying: “As to Bin’s person, he surpasses Qian by very far.
replacements.idiomatic: Chen Qian, who was present, straightened his tablet and said, “Tang Bin is far my superior as a man.

replacements.literal: ” The emperor laughed and said: “But if able to be like you, that is indeed not easily obtained—what talk of surpassing.
replacements.idiomatic: ” The emperor smiled and replied, “Merely to match you would be rare enough; we need not speak of surpassing.

replacements.literal: ” Thereupon he summoned Bin as subordinate of the armory bureau.
replacements.idiomatic: ” He thereupon appointed Tang Bin to the armory bureau.

replacements.literal: The emperor asked, saying: “By what did you achieve summons?
replacements.idiomatic: The emperor asked, “What earned you this appointment?”

replacements.literal: ” He replied, saying: “Cultivating enterprise in a mean lane, viewing the traces left by the ancients—speech fills all under Heaven without mouth fault; conduct fills all under Heaven without resentment and hatred.
replacements.idiomatic: ” He answered, “Studying in obscurity and pondering the example of the ancients: one may speak before the world without indiscretion and act before the world without earning ill will.

replacements.literal: ” The emperor looked toward the four seats and said: “The name does not travel empty.
replacements.idiomatic: ” The emperor glanced at those seated and said, “His reputation is no empty boast.

replacements.literal: ” Another day, he said to Kong Hao: “Recently I have seen Tang Bin—you have incurred the blame of concealing the worthy.”
replacements.idiomatic: ” On another occasion he told Kong Hao, “I have lately met Tang Bin; you stand charged with hiding talent from the throne.”

replacements.literal: At first, at Deng Ai’s execution, Emperor Wen because Ai had long been on Long’s right and ordinarily won the hearts of the gentry, once he was exterminated, feared border sentiment would be stirred and agitated; he sent Bin secretly to inspect it.
replacements.idiomatic: When Deng Ai was put to death, Emperor Wen feared that the Longxi frontier, where Deng had long served and enjoyed the troops’ devotion, might grow restless if he were suddenly destroyed, and secretly dispatched Tang Bin to assess the mood.

replacements.literal: Bin returned and reported to the emperor, saying: “Deng Ai was jealous and harsh, deceitful and narrow; he boasted ability and trusted talent—those who complied he called understanding of affairs; those who spoke straight he called offending contradiction.
replacements.idiomatic: Tang Bin reported, “Deng Ai was suspicious, harsh, and narrow; he prized his own abilities—flatterers he deemed astute, frank men he treated as insubordinate.

replacements.literal: Although chief clerk, major, aides, and headquarters staff—if answers missed the point, he always saw cursing and humiliation.
replacements.idiomatic: Even chief clerk, major, and camp staff faced abuse if their replies displeased him.

replacements.literal: In placing his person he lacked ritual; he greatly lost men’s hearts.
replacements.idiomatic: He treated others without courtesy and forfeited the army’s goodwill.

replacements.literal: Moreover he liked to impose labor service and repeatedly toiled the mass of laborers.
replacements.idiomatic: He also habitually imposed corvée and overworked the people.

replacements.literal: Long’s right greatly suffered bitterness from him; they delighted to hear of his disaster and were unwilling to be used by him.
replacements.idiomatic: Longxi had groaned under his rule; they welcomed his fall and would not rally to him again.

replacements.literal: Now the various armies have already arrived—sufficient to suppress inside and outside; I wish you not to take it as a worry.”
replacements.idiomatic: The imperial forces now on the scene are ample to hold the region; Your Majesty need not worry.”

replacements.literal: Soon he was appointed gentleman of the Masters of Writing for water works.
replacements.idiomatic: Shortly afterward he was named director of the Water Section in the Secretariat.

replacements.literal: At the beginning of Taishi, he was granted noble rank *guanneihou*.
replacements.idiomatic: In the first year of the Taishi era he received the title of secondary marquis.

replacements.literal: He went out to fill Ye county magistrate; Bin with virtue aligned ritual; in one full cycle he transformed and completed.
replacements.idiomatic: Posted as magistrate of Ye, he led by moral example and ritual, and within a year the district was transformed.

replacements.literal: He was promoted Yiyang grand administrator; he clearly established prohibitions and defenses; the hundred surnames were secure in it.
replacements.idiomatic: Promoted to grand administrator of Yiyang, he enforced clear laws and defenses, and the people lived at ease.

replacements.literal: Because of his mother’s mourning he left office.
replacements.idiomatic: He resigned to observe mourning for his mother.

replacements.literal: Yizhou on the east adjoined Wu raiders; the post of supervising army was vacant; court deliberation employed Wuling grand administrator Yang Zong and Bin.
replacements.idiomatic: Yizhou bordered Wu on the east; with the army supervisor’s post empty, the court debated appointing either Yang Zong, grand administrator of Wuling, or Tang Bin.

replacements.literal: Emperor Wu thereupon asked Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary Wen Li; Li said: “Zong and Bin both cannot be lost.
replacements.idiomatic: Emperor Wu consulted Wen Li, Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary, who replied, “You cannot afford to lose either Yang Zong or Tang Bin.

replacements.literal: Yet Bin has much wealth-desire, while Zong is fond of wine—only Your Majesty decides it.
replacements.idiomatic: Yet Tang Bin is acquisitive, while Yang Zong drinks heavily—the choice is yours.”

replacements.literal: ” The emperor said: “Wealth-desire can be satisfied; as for wine, it is hard to change.
replacements.idiomatic: ” The emperor said, “Greed can be curbed; a drunkard is harder to reform.”

replacements.literal: ” Thereupon he employed Bin.
replacements.idiomatic: ” He chose Tang Bin.

replacements.literal: Before long again an edict ordered Bin to supervise military affairs of Badong and all, and added General Who Extends Martial Might.
replacements.idiomatic: Soon an edict named him supervisor of military affairs in Badong with the additional title General Who Extends Martial Might.

replacements.literal: He presented a plan to attack Wu; it greatly matched the emperor’s intent.
replacements.idiomatic: His strategy for the Wu campaign matched the emperor’s wishes.

replacements.literal: Later he together with Wang Jun jointly attacked Wu; Bin encamped and held the choke point, acting as vanguard of the mass of armies.
replacements.idiomatic: Later he campaigned against Wu alongside Wang Jun, holding the key approaches and leading the van.

replacements.literal: Whenever he deployed decoy troops, responding to the moment he controlled victory; he took Xiling and Lexiang, in many cases capturing and seizing.
replacements.idiomatic: He repeatedly used feints, seized opportunities, and took Xiling and Lexiang with heavy captures.

replacements.literal: From Baling and Mian’s mouth eastward, wherever the bandits gathered, none failed to tremble in fear; they inverted halberds and bared flesh [torso].
replacements.idiomatic: East of Baling and the Han estuary every Wu stronghold quailed; defenders threw down their arms and came out bare-chested to surrender.

replacements.literal: Bin knew the bandit raiders were already exterminated; Sun Hao was about to surrender; not yet two hundred *li* to Jianye, he claimed illness and delayed, to show not competing.
replacements.idiomatic: Seeing Wu’s forces broken and Sun Hao ready to yield, he halted two hundred *li* short of Jianye, pleading illness, to avoid the scramble for glory.

replacements.literal: Indeed there were those who arrived first who quarreled over goods; those who arrived later who quarreled over merit—at that time those with understanding none failed to esteem Bin for this act.
replacements.idiomatic: As it happened, the first arrivals squabbled over booty and the latecomers over credit; informed observers all praised Tang Bin’s restraint.

replacements.literal: With Wu pacified, an edict said: “General Who Extends Martial Might Tang Bin received appointment on a frontier corner; east he resisted Wu raiders; south he supervised Man and Yue; he soothed and quieted the border fields; he had pacifying-and-controlling traces.
replacements.idiomatic: After Wu fell, an edict declared, “General Who Extends Martial Might Tang Bin held a border command: he faced Wu in the east, watched the southern tribes, and kept the marches tranquil—true pacification and control.

replacements.literal: Moreover at every turn he was stirring and forthright; his intent lay in establishing merit.
replacements.idiomatic: He was ardent by nature and bent on achievement.

replacements.literal: Recently in the expedition and suppression, supporting illness he received orders; he first opened the martial line; he presented captives and handed over severed-ear tallies; merit and effect were manifest and clear.
replacements.idiomatic: In the recent campaign he took the field despite illness, opened the advance, delivered prisoners and trophies, and his service stood out.

replacements.literal: Let Bin be made General of the Right, area commander-in-chief of military affairs of Badong and all.
replacements.idiomatic: He is appointed General of the Right and area commander for all Badong forces.

replacements.literal: ” He was summoned and appointed Colonel of the Wings of the Army, his enfeoffment changed to marquis of Shangyong county, food households six thousand, silk six thousand bolts granted.
replacements.idiomatic: ” He was recalled as Colonel of the Wings of the Army, enfeoffed as marquis of Shangyong with six thousand households and a gift of six thousand bolts of silk.

replacements.literal: When the court had doubtful deliberations, he always participated in them.
replacements.idiomatic: Whenever court debate stalled on a point, he was called in.

replacements.literal: The northern barbarians invaded and plundered Beiping; Bin was made credential bearer, supervisor of military affairs of Youzhou and all, concurrent colonel protecting the Wuhuan, general of the right.
replacements.idiomatic: Northern tribes raided Beiping; Tang Bin received the credentials, took charge of Youzhou forces, held the concurrent post of Colonel Protector of the Wuhuan, and kept his rank as General of the Right.

replacements.literal: Once Bin arrived at the command, he drilled troops and sharpened weapons, broadly farmed and weighted grain crops, shook might and displayed martial power, proclaimed and made understood the state’s commands, showed them grace and trust.
replacements.idiomatic: At his post he trained soldiers, honed weapons, promoted farming, staged demonstrations of force, published imperial policy, and combined awe with good faith.

replacements.literal: Thereupon the two Xianbei divisions Damowei and Tihe and others together sent hostage sons to enter tribute.
replacements.idiomatic: Two Xianbei confederations led by Damowei and Tihe then sent hostages and tribute.

replacements.literal: Concurrently he repaired schools; instructing and leading, he was without weariness; benevolent favor broadly spread.
replacements.idiomatic: He restored schools, taught tirelessly, and his kindness reached widely.

replacements.literal: Thereupon he opened and expanded the old border; he pushed back territory a thousand *li*.
replacements.idiomatic: He recovered old ground and pushed the frontier back a thousand *li*.

replacements.literal: He restored Qin’s long-wall barrier; from Wencheng reaching to Jieshi, stretching through mountains and valleys nearly three thousand *li*, he divided armies to garrison and hold; beacon mounds faced one another in sight.
replacements.idiomatic: He rebuilt the Qin line of wall from Wencheng to Jieshi, nearly three thousand *li* through hill country, with garrisons and beacons linked along its length.

replacements.literal: By this the borderlands obtained peace; there was no dog-barking alarm; from Han and Wei expedition commands none matched it.
replacements.idiomatic: The border knew such calm that dogs seldom barked at alarm—no frontier command since Han and Wei had matched it.

replacements.literal: The Xianbei various kinds feared; thereupon they killed Damowei.
replacements.idiomatic: The Xianbei, cowed by him, turned on Damowei and slew him.

replacements.literal: Bin wished to punish them; he feared if he listed it above and awaited reply, the barbarians would certainly scatter and flee; thereupon he issued You and Ji carts and oxen.
replacements.idiomatic: Tang Bin meant to strike them but knew a memorial and wait for approval would let the tribes scatter, so he requisitioned transport oxen from You and Ji without prior clearance.

replacements.literal: Army adviser Xu Zhi secretly memorialized it.
replacements.idiomatic: His adviser Xu Zhi reported this secretly to the throne.

replacements.literal: An edict sent the imperial secretary with a caged cart to summon Bin and deliver him to the commandant of justice; because the affair was straight he was released.
replacements.idiomatic: The court sent a censor to haul him to the capital in a prison cart, but the commandant of justice cleared him as acting within right.

replacements.literal: The hundred surnames pursued and admired Bin’s merit and virtue; while living they for him set up a stele and made praise.
replacements.idiomatic: The people, grateful for his rule, erected a monument and composed a eulogy while he still lived.

replacements.literal: Bin at first received learning from Yan De of Donghai; disciples were very many; alone he eyed Bin as having hall-and-temple talent.
replacements.idiomatic: Tang Bin had studied under Yan De of Donghai amid a large school; alone Yan marked him as material for high office.

replacements.literal: When Bin’s office was accomplished, De had already died; thereupon he for him set up a stele.
replacements.idiomatic: By the time Tang Bin’s career flourished, Yan De was dead; Tang therefore raised a stele in his honor.

replacements.literal: At the beginning of Yuankang, he was appointed credential bearer, general of the van, concurrent colonel of the western Rong, Yongzhou inspector.
replacements.idiomatic: Early in Yuankang he became credential bearer, General of the Van, concurrent Colonel of the Western Rong, and inspector of Yongzhou.

replacements.literal: He issued instruction, saying: “This province is a famous capital; gentry men are forest and marsh.
replacements.idiomatic: He proclaimed, “Yongzhou is a renowned seat; its scholars gather like trees in a grove.”

replacements.literal: Recluses Huangfu Shenshen, Yan Shulong, Jiang Maoshi, Liang Ziyuan and others together had intent and integrity clear and subtle, conduct and practice lofty and pure.
replacements.idiomatic: The recluses Huangfu Shenshen, Yan Shulong, Jiang Maoshi, and Liang Ziyuan combine sterling principle with spotless lives.”

replacements.literal: Treading the territory and gazing at the wind, I am empty-hearted and hunger-thirst; I think to add summoning and bringing, treating them with the canon of not treating as subjects.
replacements.idiomatic: I have long admired them and wish to invite them with the etiquette reserved for guests, not subjects.”

replacements.literal: With headcloth we meet; we discuss the Way—that is all—how could with clerk duties I bend and stain lofty norms.
replacements.idiomatic: We shall meet informally and speak of principle; I would not demean their high standard with petty bureaucratic demands.”

replacements.literal: Commanderies and kingdoms shall complete ritual and dispatch them, to match the prefecture-city’s hope.
replacements.idiomatic: Let each district prepare proper escort and send them forward, as the capital expects.”

replacements.literal: ” Thereupon the four men all arrived; Bin respected and treated them.
replacements.idiomatic: ” All four came; Tang Bin received them with respect.

replacements.literal: He died in office; at the time his years were sixty; his posthumous title was Xiang; two hundred bolts of silk and two hundred thousand cash were granted.
replacements.idiomatic: He died in post at sixty, posthumously titled Xiang, with two hundred bolts of silk and two hundred thousand cash granted for his funeral.

replacements.literal: The eldest son succeeded; office reached Guangling grand administrator.
replacements.idiomatic: His eldest son succeeded him and rose to grand administrator of Guangling.

replacements.literal: The younger son Qi, General Who Conquers the Barbarians’ major.
replacements.idiomatic: His younger son Tang Qi became a major on the staff of the General Who Conquers the Barbarians.

replacements.literal: Shiping
replacements.idiomatic: Shiping

replacements.literal: The historians say: The Sun clan bore river-and-mountain’s blocking separation, relied on Ox-and-Dipper’s unlucky miasma, suddenly possessed the water country, and resisted the superior state.
replacements.idiomatic: The historians remark: The Sun house leaned on the Yangtze’s barrier and the dire omens over the Wu stars, seized the lake country, and defied the central court.

replacements.literal: The two Wangs attached to the moment of armies, received the baton and swiftly campaigned; Hun already presented victory at Hengjiang; Jun also conquered and cleared Jianye.
replacements.idiomatic: The two Wangs took the field under orders: Wang Hun won at Hengjiang, Wang Jun swept Jianye.

replacements.literal: At that time in the campaign of punishing Wu, though generals and commanders were many, the merit of settling Wu, here was the foremost.
replacements.idiomatic: Among the many commanders in the Wu expedition, theirs was the decisive share in finishing the war.

replacements.literal: If only they had enlarged Fan-father’s not boasting, emulated Yangxia’s pushing merit, above reported to the temple hall, below relied on generals and soldiers.
replacements.idiomatic: Had they honored Fan Wenzi’s habit of disclaiming merit and the Yangxia gentry’s willingness to yield credit, informing the high ministers above and trusting the commanders and troops below,

replacements.literal: Would it not be luxuriant merit luxuriant virtue, those who begin well and end well!
replacements.idiomatic: would they not have paired brilliant achievement with lasting virtue and matched a worthy end to a worthy beginning?

replacements.literal: This they did not preserve; that is what they strove for.
replacements.idiomatic: Instead they abandoned that path and chased lesser quarrels.

replacements.literal: Some boasted merit and bore pride; some relied on power and acted arrogant; vying they framed Southern Dipper, completed this shell-brocade.
replacements.idiomatic: Some swaggered over their feats, others threw their weight about; together they wove slanders like the “Southern Dipper” ode and the “shell-patterned brocade” calumny.

replacements.literal: Thereupon they clamored and defiled the imperial seat, disrupted and disordered constant norms; already they became a warning to meritorious ministers, also incurred ridicule in pure opinion—how not regrettable!
replacements.idiomatic: They fouled the throne with wrangling, broke orderly relations, warned future generals against pride, and earned the censure of every fair judge—a pity indeed.

replacements.literal: Wang Ji then was arrogant at father’s narrow heart, contrary to disputing son’s clear right—outstanding talent though many, what use also!
replacements.idiomatic: Wang Ji aped his father’s pettiness and abandoned the decency a son owes—talent avails little without character.

replacements.literal: Tang Bin feared and avoided cross quarrels, attached illness and delayed; retiring yielding wind—worthier than Hun and Jun by far.
replacements.idiomatic: Tang Bin shunned the quarrel, lingered on pretext of illness, and showed a humility that puts Wang Hun and Wang Jun to shame.

replacements.literal: The biography says “not constrained by conduct inspection”—how could that obtain an elder’s conduct!
replacements.idiomatic: Yet the text calls him “unconcerned with propriety”—that is hardly the mark of a true gentleman.

replacements.literal: The praise says: The two Wangs commanded armies; Huai and sea together.
replacements.idiomatic: The encomium runs: “Two Wangs held the hosts; Huai and sea bowed as one.”

replacements.literal: Hun already harmed the good; Jun also boasted merit.
replacements.idiomatic: Hun injured the worthy; Jun preened over his deeds.

replacements.literal: Wuzi was a heroic outstanding man; early he joined the court ranks.
replacements.idiomatic: Wang Ji, a swaggering blade, long sat in court.

replacements.literal: He vented desire at Ox-heart, wound sentiment at horse levee.
replacements.idiomatic: He chased rare dishes and poured passion into the polo bank.

replacements.literal: The Confucian exemplar knew retiring; avoiding name he preserved integrity.
replacements.idiomatic: Tang Bin, the gentleman who knew retreat, shunned fame and kept his honor whole.
